newsitem.title: USA: political slugger takes one on jaw.
newsitem.headline: political slugger takes one on jaw.

text.p: The trouble with Newt Gingrich, many would say, is that he did not practice what he preached.

Gingrich, 53, a Georgia Republican once without peer as a crusader for strict congressional ethics and a scourge of Democratic violators, felt the lash himself Tuesday when the House of Representatives voted to reprimand and fine him -- its leader -- for admitted ethics breaches of his own.
Thus did he become the first House speaker formally punished by vote of his colleagues for misconduct in office.

That did not strip him of his prestigious leadership post, second in line of succession to the U.S. presidency after Vice President Al Gore. But much of his formidable political influence has clearly evaporated, and it is a humbled, philosophical Gingrich in the speaker's chair these days.
"To the degree I was too brash, too self-confident or too pushy, I apologise," he said two weeks ago after the House grudgingly re-elected him its speaker.

Putting aside the gloating of Democrats at what they see as a delicious comeuppance, it is plain many Republicans are furious at Gingrich for putting the party in this position and forcing them to take sides in a major public embarrassment.
He barely won the speaker vote despite heavy arm-twisting of Republicans. A few of his troops jumped ship anyway.

And that was before release of a scathing investigative report that was the basis for Tuesday's punishment vote. It said his questionable use of tax-exempt money for lectures some saw as politically flavored reflected a pattern "of disregard and disrespect for (proper) standards of conduct."
He conceded "with great sadness" last December that he had failed to get proper legal advice on use of charitable funds to finance the lecture course and misled the House about this.
Addition of the $300,000 penalty showed his colleagues, Republican and Democrat, did not think a reprimand sufficient.
Inevitably there is speculation in Washington Gingrich might quit the leadership post before his two-year term is up.
But he has given no public sign of that. And he remains a political force, able and shrewd if also sadder and wiser.

It is all quite a turnabout for a cocky conqueror who seized the speakership by right two years ago as architect of an election triumph that gave Republicans their first two-house congressional majorities in 40 years.
He became Time magazine's "Man of the Year" cover boy and was much discussed as a potential 1996 Republican presidential candidate.
He had risen as a politician who never shrank from a political brawl and made his name, especially, as an ethics warrior before and after election to Congress in 1978.
His most celebrated victory in that line was in leading the drive that forced Democratic Speaker Jim Wright to resign from Congress because of ethics charges in 1989.

But there were other episodes too. He pushed for the expulsion of Democratic Representative Charles Diggs of Michigan, who was eventually censured for misuse of congressional funds in 1979. He persuaded the House to upgrade the punishments of Democrat Gerry Studds of Massachusetts and Republican Dan Crane of Illinois from reprimand to censure on sexual misconduct charges in 1983.
Democrats also bitterly recall Gingrich's early portrayals of Congress under their majority rule as corrupt and venal. He made one such attack in front of a federal prison for effect.
Power brought him his own controversies. He accepted a $4.5 million advance for his book, "To Renew America," then bowed to widespread criticism and turned down the advance.
He also made some tactical political blunders.

His pursuit of conservative reform proposals embedded in his "Contract with America" enabled Democrats to demonise him in last year's election as a heartless elitist who wanted to slash Medicare health insurance for the elderly and disabled.

Two partial shutdowns of the U.S. government in a budget dispute with President Bill Clinton last winter -- for which many voters blamed the Republicans -- helped reduce the party's House majority in the election.
Gingrich was born June 17, 1943, in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. He is married and has two grown daughters from a first marriage that ended in divorce.
